messages.text: Here, {gift_item}. The right tool in the right hand saves a lot of trouble.
Take {gift_item}. Keep it useful and it will repay you twice.
Then the advice had a good edge. {tested_villager} liked {gift_item}.
Wrong tool for the work. For {gift_subject}, use {alternative_gift} instead.
{gift_item} slipped in the hand? Try {alternative_gift}; cleaner work.
Wrong tool, wrong job. Pick up {alternative_gift} next time.
You used the advice as-is? Hm. Sharpen your judgment and bring {alternative_gift}.

openings.text: Mind the smithing table. What do you need?

closings.text: Back to making tools that do not fail, then.

lines.text: Cracked handles are small warnings with expensive timing.
A dull edge makes every simple job into a bad plan.
A good tool is quiet proof that someone cared before trouble started.
Mind the table. Good tools begin with nobody bumping my elbow.
A handle should fit the hand, not argue with it.
A sharp edge is useful. A careless one is just trouble with shine.
I once fixed a pick that had seen more stone than sense.
Tool jokes work better when they have a point. Mine sometimes have two.
That idea is bent past repair.
The bench hears every complaint before the finished tool gets praised.
Cracked handles are warnings. Ignore them and they become stories.
A shovel broke on me once because I asked it to do axe work.
You are using your manners like the wrong tool for the job.

pacify.text: Fine. I will put the edge away, for now.
Wrong measure. It takes {emerald_cost} {emeralds} to set this right.
No. You are using emeralds like the wrong tool.
